en: Itivuttaka 36 Dukanipāta, Paṭhamavagga Thus it was said by the Blessed One; having been said by the Sublime One, it was so heard by me: “Monks, there are these two kinds of persons found existing in the world. What two? The one who is intent on his own welfare, but not on the welfare of others; and the one who is intent on the welfare of others, but not on his own welfare. These, monks, are the two kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Happy One rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had departed, a certain monk approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “It was said by the Blessed One: ‘Monks, there are these two kinds of persons found existing in the world…’ Now, how is the person intent on his own welfare, but not on the welfare of others, to be understood? “Here, monk, a certain person dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, burning with sensual lust, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust within himself. He dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will, burning with ill will, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen ill will within himself. He dwells with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor, burning with sloth and torpor, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sloth and torpor within himself.

He dwells with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse, burning with restlessness and remorse, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen restlessness and remorse within himself. He dwells with a mind obsessed by doubt, burning with doubt, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt within himself. This, monk, is called the person intent on his own welfare, but not on the welfare of others. And how, monk, is the person intent on the welfare of others, but not on his own welfare, to be understood? Here, monk, a certain person dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, burning with sensual lust, yet he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust within himself. He dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... doubt, burning with doubt, yet he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt within himself. This, monk, is called the person intent on the welfare of others, but not on his own welfare. These, monk, are the two kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Happy One rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then that monk, having understood the meaning of what was said by the Blessed One, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed for his own dwelling. There, in private, that monk reflected on the meaning of what was said by the Blessed One. As he reflected, the hair on his body stood on end. He thought: “It is wonderful, it is marvelous! How the Blessed One has explained this matter so well. Indeed, the Blessed One is the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the disciples of the Blessed One is practicing the good way. Then that monk, having attained confidence in the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, attained the fruit of stream-entry. And that monk became one of the stream-enterers. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having been said by the Sublime One, it was so heard by me. Therefore, this was said: “One intent on his own welfare, but not on the welfare of others; One intent on the welfare of others, but not on his own welfare— These two kinds of persons are found existing in the world; But the one who is intent on both is the best among men. The Second Discourse on Deceitful Behavior Toward People.
This was said by the Blessed One; thus have I heard:

"Monks, this holy life is not lived for the sake of deceiving people, nor for the sake of flattering people, nor for the sake of gain, honor, and renown as a reward, nor with the thought, 'Let people know me thus.'"
"Furthermore, monks, this holy life is lived for the sake of direct knowledge and for the sake of full understanding.
Thus the Blessed One spoke. With reference to this, it is said:
“For the sake of direct knowledge and for the sake of full understanding,
that Blessed One taught the holy life, which is not based on mere tradition.”
Leading to the unfathomable depths of Nibbāna—
this is the path followed by the great ones, the great seers.
Whoever practices according to what has been taught by the Buddha will make an end of suffering.
“Those who act according to the Teacher’s instruction.
This matter was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
